questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I always knew I wanted to go on an exchange, hopefully outside of Europe. I dreamed about going to Australia, New Zealand or Canada and ended up choosing Canada because it looks amazing in pictures and the people should be some of the kindest - so I really wanted to experience that!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: McMaster University is located in Hamilton, and Hamilton is not that interesting at all... Besides Hamilton, the campus of McMaster University is full of life and so is the lovely small town, Westdale, just nearby. I spend all my time with my friends on campus and in Westdale at the local bar or one of the cafes. And the time spent with them either at the campus, in Westdale or travelling around Canada makes my overall study abroad experience almost perfect - the only downside for me is the city of Hamilton.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It's a long process to go on exchange, no matter where you have to go! You will have to do some things more than twice and you will be tempted to give up - but please don't. Eventually, everything will work out fine, because most people really want to help exchange students. Upon arrival, it can be tricky tho. I used the fact sheet from the University of Copenhagen a lot to see what I had to do and when. And by the help of the Mobility Online system, everything is quite easy to follow. But information such as courses, where to stay in Canada, visa and so on, was quite tricky. It was possible to attend some summer webinars about visas and the city of Hamilton and so on, which I found very useful but it wasn't really proclaimed anywhere (as far as I can remember), but if you surf around on the website of the university for long enough - then you will eventually end up with something useful. 
Besides this, we got several emails from the university with different deadlines and links to different sites that might be good to know - and they mentioned an app (iCent), which was also quite informative in some ways. 

Look for 'International Student Services' and 'Mac incoming'

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I attended the so-called MOOSE trip right before the semester began. It is a tour for international- and exchange students organized by the McMaster Outdoor club (highly recommended to keep an eye out on their trips!). On this tour, I met a lot of new international and exchange students and some of the students from McMaster University, who helped answer a lot of questions about everything (mostly non-academical stuff). Besides this trip, the international student services held an event where they went through some of the more practical stuff about the courses (how much you need to pass a course), the university clubs, insurance, safety and so on.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The only thing is, that you might have to be persistent and send multiple emails to get ahold of the right person to answer your question.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding off-campus housing was one of the most stressful and difficult things to do! Travel to Hamilton before the semester starts!!! Respond to a lot of Facebook posts, and make one about yourself where you tell a little bit about who you are and the situation you are in - and then cross your fingers and most of all, go out and see the places and meet the people before you make any decisions! You really have to be patient and use your common sense when looking through Facebook groups (unfortunately there are a lot of scammers out there) - I had my luck with this group 'Westdale neighbourhood'. 
First of all, the location matters! I would definitely recommend living in Westdale since it is within walking distance of campus and it is a safe and lovely small town with lots of students at the cafes. 
Next up is that you might have to compromise on some things. Make it clear for yourself if you want to live in student housing or private with a family or try to find your own thing - no matter what, embrace yourself for the expensive rent and make sure to have a contract with your landlord! 
Finally, if you end up in downtown Hamilton it is not the end of the world. You are closer to the party clubs and 'Hess Village' (an area with a few restaurants and bars/clubs), but the struggle is the public transport to and from campus. The public transportation works it is just not that reliable and you might have to wait a long time on a bus (so having to take two connected busses is not recommendable).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I loved living off-campus! I lived with a 96-year-old lady who was the most loving person I have ever met. Living with her of course had some downsides, but overall it was a wonderful thing to get to know her and her family. And having my "own home" where I could invite my friends over for dinner was just lovely. 
But you have to keep in mind that it is expensive to rent and the bills can also be expensive - but everything depends on the contract you make with your landlord, so do yourself the favour of reading through contracts and making sure that you are not responsible for things you wouldn't be responsible for in Denmark if you rented a place.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was super difficult and a long and tiring process to find a place to stay. So be patient, go to Canada around 2 weeks before the semester starts to search for off-campus housing (if you want that) and to attend the MOOSE trip (a few international and exchange students from this trip found something together, but the market is intense and there are not a lot of empty houses/apartments with an affordable rent that close to campus).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
To be registered at McMaster University was not that difficult. After I send the application through KU and it got approved there was some information from ucphabroad at KU. After that, I had to wait for a while before I got an email from the host institution. Within this email, there was a link to another portal (just like Mobility Online), where I had to do the application at McMaster University. After a little while, this also got approved and then I was registered at the host institution. 
According to the courses, it was a confusing process. Because I was going during Fall 2022, the only course catalogue available at the time we had to request the courses we wanted was from Fall 2021, so some courses might have been removed or changed or even added by the time we were gonna be at campus. Finding courses that sounded interesting took a very long time and I looked through a lot of course descriptions (4-5 lines about the course content). When I had requested the 8 courses that were mandatory to request, time went by and then I got an email from the Science department with some information about whom to contact regarding course approvals. It is necessary to get the courses approved by the academic advisor of your faculty before you can enroll in them (which was a whole process alone). After final enrollment in the courses you are ready to begin the studies at McMaster University - but only a week or so, after the beginning of the term, the 'add-and-drop' period ends, which makes the first period of time really stressful if you are not satisfied with the courses you have chosen before you came. So pro tip: for your own sake, get a lot of courses approved by the University of Copenhagen, before you go and make sure to reach out to your academic advisor at McMaster as soon as you know, that you wanna switch to a new course.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You get an email with information about your academic advisor which is very helpful in the whole course registration process. Besides that Google; "McMaster University courses" --> "Programs, Future Students" is where I found most of the things I needed to know.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Because we had to look at an outdated course catalogue, two of my courses were not available by the time I attended McMaster University. But in the end, I ended up with four useful courses - some better than others. I would have preferred to change one of my courses, but unfortunately, that wasn't a possibility in combination with the other three courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patient in the registration process and begin to look at courses as soon as possible so you have an idea of a plan B or plan C if you end up in that situation. And send as many emails with questions to your academic advisor as you feel like - they are there to help and it can be really tricky to figure out their system, so take all the help you can!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: All four courses I had was level 3 courses, which means that the academic level is supposed to be around the level of our courses at this time in our BA. One of my courses was an introductory course, which was seen at the academic level. It was way easier and less technical to follow this course compared to the other three. Even tho the academic level was lower, I still learned a lot and I really liked the professor and the TA of this course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The biggest difference is the midterms which are minor exams that test you on the stuff you have been learning up until this point (around half the course). In some of the courses, there are also a few assignments and/or presentations (either individually or in groups). Altogether, the presence of midterms, the smaller assignments, presentations and quizzes during the courses, meant that you have to keep up a bit more during the term since the midterms counted 25-35% of your final grade, but also that the final exam wasn't all-or-nothing.
Overall, the academic level was lower than here in Denmark - they don't expect equally as much of you - but there are more "tests" along the way, but that just means that you can pass a lot of the course before the final exam and then you don't have to study for two weeks before the final exam to pass the course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
HTHSCI 3K03 - Principles of Virology (elective)
LIFESCI 3G03 - Introduction to Epidemiology (elective)
LIFESCI 3BB3 - Neurobiology of Disease (limited elective)
MOLBIOL 3O03 - Microbial Genetics (limited elective)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I personally liked the Epidemiology course because it's something different from what you can get back here in Denmark. It wasn't a challenging course at all which meant that I had time to do other things as well (win-win).
Principles of Virology was great because of the professor (Dr. Caitlin E. Mullarkey Dphil). Her enthusiasm for the subject and her knowledge made it all way more interesting than I think I would have found it otherwise. 
Neurobiology of Disease was a great course if you like to get invested in the local community. The professor in this course made it a part of the course to do a 'community engagement group project' on one of three different subjects presented in class - overall a really great idea and a lovely way to get connected with other students, but if you get together with other international- or exchange students it might be a bit difficult to engage yourself fully (which was the case for me). And personally, I regretted every moment of Microbial genetics because I didn't find it interesting - but once again the professor here was a really enthusiastic young woman who loved to teach with made it durable.

Housing DKK per month *

Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Mobile deals were more expensive than I anticipated and so was meat - but overall is Canada quite expensive, so everything was pricy.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It is recommendable to spend a day or two to go on a bigger shopping trip at Walmart (which will be more expensive than you anticipate), but also worth it. You can get home with pots and pans, wardrobes, pyjamas and lots of food and snacks. When travelling around Canada, I found that hostels were cheaper than I expected. And otherwise my "other fees" includes trips with McOutdoor club and a self-planned trip to the Rookie Mountains and so on.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The only thing missing non-academically would be more events arranged by campus for a mix of international and exchange students together with locals. The international student services are really good at making different things for people who study abroad, but if you wanted to attend an event for a mix of locals and internationals you had to seek that yourself.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were all kinds of non-academic opportunities. Go to the 'club fair' at the beginning of the term to see what kinds of clubs McMaster University has to offer. There is something for everyone! And if you don't want to join anything that's also completely fine. Just keep your eyes and ears open and then you will find something that sounds fun.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Together with other international and exchange students we created a team and joined the Intramurals soccer tournament and played a match every once a week for a month or so - that was one of the best decisions I made!
Besides the athletic aspect McOutdoor was amazing. I joined both the MOOSE trip and the trip to Algonquin park and both of them are worth paying for (even tho they are expensive) - so if you like nature, canoeing, and getting to know your friends while freezing in a tent or complaining over the wind while canoeing then go go go!
Otherwise attending dinners for international students is also recommendable.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend you to go to Montreal on a weekend trip and go to 'The Big West' (the Rookie Mountains) around Vancouver and the national parks Banff, Jasper and Whistler when going to Canada!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy to adjust to the local culture of Canada. Everyone is super sweet, helpful and lovely. And after the MOOSE trip, the likelihood of you getting some new friends, that might even be danish, is pretty big - and these are gonna be your safety blanket for the first couple of weeks when everything is still new.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I personally socialized with local students between classes when I discovered that there were a few people that I had more than one course with. Otherwise, attend the stadium on game day, sit around campus or just by sitting at cafes in Westdale. If you want to socialize with local students, there are a lot of opportunities.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The main cultural difference was that the Canadian people are very polite and even a stranger on the bus will compliment your shoes if they like them. Besides this, they say thank you when they leave the bus, which was kinda weird at the beginning. And then you have to be aware of the tipping culture - you tip everyone, everywhere, always..

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The politeness and helpfulness of the Candian people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Travel to Canada before the beginning of the semester to search for accommodation, if you want to live off-campus!
Go on the MOOSE trip, which is also before the semester begins. This is an expensive trip and things could be better, but this is a great way to get to know other people who are gonna be there for the next 4-12 months as well. You will not regret going when you look back and see that the friendships made on that trip are the ones you enjoyed for the whole semester.
Be sure to explore other parts of Canada as well and then just enjoy a beer or two with your people at the local bar (Snooty Fox) whenever the time is there.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be aware that the courses you are choosing from are from an old catalogue so make sure you have a long list of courses to choose from and get them all pre-approved from KU before you go, so you are ready to change your course within the limited add-and-drop period - the courses have to be approved by the host institution as well, so if you have to wait for approval from KU and then from McMaster, you are possibly not gonna make it in time before the deadline. 

Look at places you wanna go in Hamilton, Ontario or Canada in general before you go, so you can get together with some friends quite early and try to plan different trips.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was definitely the self-planned roadtrip with 6 friends around 'The Big West' of Canada - amazing nature and a lovely way to spend time with your friends. 
Besides that, it was all the small things like meeting up with friends between classes, sitting at the campus the whole day because of the different schedules we all had and then ending up going to Phoenix (a restaurant on campus) to eat and grab a beer or two or even attend the trivia night every Tuesday. Going to a party at some of the other exchange students' houses was also a huge part of the unforgettable exchange period I had.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge for me was definitely finding a place to live off-campus. It took time, a lot of effort and disappointments and I could have never imagined that I ended up in the situation I did. It had its pros and cons but overall I got lucky. And you will need a bit of luck and a lot of hard work to find the "perfect place" to stay when going on exchange.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I am truly grateful for the opportunity to go on exchange and I would do it again in a heartbeat if it was possible. So even tho it can seem scary and like a lot of hard work (because it is), then it is all worth it when you get back home, so go go go!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
